text: Bakshi Ghulam Mohammad (20 July 1907 – 15 July 1972) was an Indian politician who served as the prime minister of Jammu and Kashmir from 1953 to 1964, holding the longest continuous tenure of any prime minister or chief minister in the state's post-independence history and is recognized as a period of stability. Born in 1907 in a lower middle-class family in the Safakadal area of Srinagar, within the then princely state of Jammu and Kashmir, he had a father, Abdul Ghaffar Bakshi, who was unemployed, and six siblings—four brothers and two sisters. He received education at C.M.S Tyndale Biscoe School up to the eighth grade, which was considered a reasonable qualification at the time. He began his career as a school teacher in Christian missionary schools in Skardu and Leh, and due to family pressure, returned to Srinagar to marry. In 1925, he joined the Kashmir branch of the All India Spinners’ Association and worked as a karyakarta at Gandhi Ashram in Srinagar, founded on Mahatma Gandhi’s principles for rural development, where he was exposed to the Indian National Congress and Gandhi’s ideas, earning the epithet "Kashmiri Gandhi" for advocating the boycott of British goods. In 1927, he joined Sheikh Mohammed Abdullah in the agitation for civic and political rights for Kashmir's Muslim population, leading to the formation of the Muslim Conference, where he demonstrated organizational talent by mobilizing students and workers and establishing unions; he was arrested multiple times, including for sixteen months in Reasi sub-jail, and earned the sobriquet "Khalid-e-Kashmir" within the party. By 1938, with demands for responsible government spreading across communities, the Muslim Conference was renamed the National Conference, and Bakshi worked underground to evade state police. In 1946, during the "Quit Kashmir" movement, he escaped to British India when arrested and traveled widely to build public support for the Kashmir agitation; after Mahatma Gandhi’s visit to Kashmir in August 1947, the warrant against him was withdrawn, and he returned home after seventeen months. On 30 October 1947, Sheikh Mohammed Abdullah was appointed Head of Emergency Administration as Kashmir faced attacks from Pakistani raiders, and Bakshi became his deputy head. In March 1948, the administration was upgraded to a popular interim government, and Bakshi was given the Home portfolio. After the 1951 constituency assembly elections, Abdullah was elected prime minister and Bakshi was appointed deputy prime minister. In August 1953, Sheikh Mohammed Abdullah was dismissed and arrested with the help of the head of state Karan Singh, and Bakshi Ghulam Mohammad became prime minister, winning a unanimous vote of confidence in October and also becoming president of the National Conference by majority vote of the State Cabinet. During his tenure, the famous Kashmir Conspiracy Case was initiated against Abdullah and others. Bakshi proved to be an effective administrator and is remembered as the "Architect of Modern Kashmir" for his role in advancing the ideal of "Naya Kashmir," establishing direct rapport with people at the grassroots, and gaining widespread popularity across regions. Politically, he faced a strong challenge from the Plebiscite Front, formed by Sheikh Abdullah’s loyalists in 1955. In May 1963, after losing three parliamentary by-elections, the Congress party, under the Kamaraj plan, recommended that some ministers resign to focus on party work; Jawaharlal Nehru made the final decision, and Nehru suggested Bakshi resign. Upon Bakshi’s recommendation, Khwaja Shamsuddin, a loyalist, was appointed to succeed him, but Shamsuddin led the state only briefly. In 1964, Bakshi headed the opposition to Chief Minister Ghulam Mohammed Sadiq; in the late summer of that year, the majority of legislators compelled him to move a vote of no-confidence against the government, but he was arrested and detained under the Defence of India Rules despite having majority support from MLAs, and the assembly was prorogued by the governor. He was released on health grounds in December. In June 1965, he announced his decision to retire from politics. In the 1967 Indian general election, he was elected to the Lok Sabha from the Srinagar constituency on a National Conference ticket, defeating the ruling Congress nominee, Ali Mohammed Tariq, by a large margin, and remained a member until 1971. Bakshi Ghulam Mohammad died on 9 July 1972. He steadfastly resisted any attempts to undermine Jammu and Kashmir's special status within the Union of India.
